analytic.title: Impact of fish stocking on Eurasian otter (Lutra lutra) densities: A case study on two salmonid streams

div.p: Stocking of fish into streams is a common practice in fisheries management to increase the yield for anglers and support fish populations. European otter (Lutra lutra) predation on fish stocks of both economical and recreational value causes conflicts in many European countries. However, these stocking activities may also attract additional predators to a site. This case study aimed to investigate whether stocking of fish leads to higher otter densities in linear freshwater habitats in Central Europe. Otter faeces and data on fish stocks were collected in the province of Lower Austria along two salmonid streams, which differ considerably in fisheries management strategies. We used non-invasive genetic sampling (NGS) methods (genetic analysis of otter faeces) to ascertain otter individuals. Prey fish populations were assessed comparing length frequencies and fish biomass obtained from electrofishing series and data on stocking measures. Individual identification and socio-spatial organisation of resident otters revealed similar otter densities for both streams with 0.22 and 0.23 resident adult otters per stream kilometre. Length frequency distribution and biomass of fish indicated disappearance of stocked specimen at the time of electrofishing surveys and showed no significant difference of fish stocks between the streams. These results suggest that stocking activities may not affect the number of otter territories along the two streams studied, because availability of stocked fish is limited to angling season. We conclude that stocked streams may provide seasonally important food resources for otters, but raise the question whether stocked fish substantially contribute to the diet to raise carrying capacity for otters in linear freshwater habitats throughout a year. Furthermore we discuss the efficiency of stocking measures in streams where both self-sustaining fish populations and fish-eating predators occur.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: After being close to extinction in parts of Central Europe during the second half of the 20th century (Mason and Macdonald, 1986), Eurasian otter (Lutra lutra) populations have started to recover and within the last 20 years the range of distribution and population densities have increased due to species protection and conservation efforts (Chanin, 2003). With increasing otter numbers, fishermen have started to report economic losses related to otter predation. The historic conflict between anglers, fish farmers and this fish-eating mammal has resurfaced again and otters have come into the focus of public interest in many parts of Europe (Bodner, 1995). Especially small streams of the trout and grayling region are favoured for recreational angling on the one hand, and providing suitable habitats for otters on the other. But despite otter predation on commercially valuable fish being a controversial and emotionally discussed issue, it has scarcely been investigated (Ludwig et al., 2002;Jacobsen, 2005). To increase the yield for anglers, stocking of fish (mainly domesticated hatchery strains) has become a common practice in fisheries management (Baer et al., 2007;Pinter, 2008;Unfer and Pinter, 2010). However, in most cases the efficiency of stocking measures and the fate of stocked fish remain unknown, but there is some evidence that hatchery-reared fish may be particularly vulnerable to predators (Dieperink et al., 2001;Aarestrup et al., 2005). Furthermore the presence of stocked fish may attract additional predators to the site (Stewart et al., 2005). Previous studies show that the availability of prey influences presence and density of otters, and has distinct effects on breeding period and success, carrying capacity, mortality as well as spatio-temporal utilisation of resources; this is consistant with the assumption that otters are food-limited (Kruuk et al., 1993;Ruiz-Olmo et al., 2001;Sulkava, 2006;Kruuk 2006;Lanszki et al., 2010;Ruiz-Olmo et al., 2011). As otters predominantly feed on fish (Mason and Macdonald, 1986;Taastrøm and Jacobsen, 1999;Kruuk, 2006), changes in fish stocks and therefore food availability should hence affect otter numbers.

For otters as an elusive, mainly nocturnal species it is, however, difficult to obtain accurate estimates of population size. Thus, the development of genetic analyses of non-invasive samples during the past years provided a valuable tool for studying otters requiring no direct contact to the animals (Taberlet et al., 1996;Coxon et al., 1999;Taberlet and Luikart, 1999;Kruuk, 2006). Meanwhile challenges in non-invasive genetics related to typically low DNA quality and quantity of DNA samples (Taberlet et al., 1999) have been widely overcome by successive optimisation of field and laboratory protocols (Pompanon et al., 2005;Beja-Pereira et al., 2009;Hájková et al., 2009;Hausknecht et al., 2010). By genotyping faecal otter samples collected in the field these techniques proved to produce reliable data for otter censuses: In comparison to classic field surveys like snow tracking, NGS combined with capture-markrecapture (CMR) analysis lead to equal results in linear habitats along streams and was superior in complex habitats with high otter densities (e.g. fish pond areas) (Hájková et al., 2009) or generally when applied in large study areas (Arrendal et al., 2007). A strong point of molecular methods compared to field surveys is the supply of additional information on sex ratio, spatial organisation and relatedness. Hence, NGS has successfully been applied to estimate otter numbers and their socio-spatial organisation (e.g. Hung et al., 2004;Prigioni et al., 2006;Lanszki et al. 2008), to monitor reintroduction programmes (Koelewijn et al., 2010), and to infer genetic structure of recovered populations (Janssens et al., 2008).

To evaluate the impact of fish stocking and therefore altered food availability on otter populations we compared otter numbers and densities, their spatial and social organisation and data on fish stocks in two salmonid streams which differ considerably in fisheries management strategies. For the named advantages regarding NGS we chose to assess otter numbers along riverine habitats by genotyping otter faeces and applying capture-mark-recapture analysis. We assume that changes in fish biomass, fish species composition and abundance influence the amount and availability of food resources for otters. Further we hypothesise higher otter density and therefore a higher number of otter territories in riverine habitats with higher food availability, i.e. higher fish biomass, whereas in areas without intensive stocking a dynamic balance between prey and predator numbers in terms of otters and wild fish populations can be supposed. Hence, the aim of this study is to investigate interactions between fisheries management strategies, condition of fish stocks and otter numbers.

div.head: Study sites
div.p: Otter faeces (spraints) and data on fish stocks were collected along two salmonid streams in the province of Lower Austria: a) Kleiner Kamp and b) Große Ysper (Fig. 1). The studied area covered 18.3 km of Kleiner Kamp and 21.5 km of Große Ysper (Fig. 1, 1). As studies on otter distribution indicate both sites are representing riverine habitats, which have been repopulated by otters for more than 20 years (Kranz, 1995;Kranz et al., 2001;Kranz and Poledník, 2009). Furthermore, both study sites are situated within the siliceous Bohemian mountains and have similar stream widths and flow regimes (Table 1) (Fink et al., 2000;Haunschmid and Weiss, 2005). Existence of surrounding water bodies, notably fishponds, is comparable between the study sites, both in number and density. According to the longitudinal zonation of running waters (Illies, 1961) and the ichthyological classification, the river stretches investigated belong to the epi-and metarhithral. Thus, the native fish fauna is dominated by brown trout (Salmo trutta) and bullhead (Cottus gobio).

Besides considering hydromorphological comparability as described above, these two study sites were chosen because of differences in fisheries management practices. Kleiner Kamp undergoes a sustainable, ecologically oriented management including the abandonment of stocking fish and harvest regulations considering natural productivity (annual average fish harvest about 0.3 kg/km (G. Unfer, personal observation, 2014). In the fishing beats of Große Ysper hatchery fish are stocked periodically during the fishing season from April to September. Usually brown trout, rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) and brook trout (Salvelinus fontinalis) in catchable sizes (>250 mm total length) are released. All three species are stocked in equal proportions and the total annual amount of stocked fish ranges from 25 to 45 kg/km, the average fish harvest, i.e. fish caught by angling, is about 3 kg/km (A. Pöcksteiner, personal communication, 2011).

Brown trout as the dominant species in our study sites particularly requires structures along the riverbanks, which provide shelter and hardly frequent open water zones in streams (Armstrong et al., 2003;Klemetsen et al., 2003). Accordingly, to supply their needs otters have to adapt the shape of home ranges to given habitat conditions (Ó Néill et al., 2009). Therefore, we chose to present otter densities and fish biomass in oligotrophic salmonid streams per stream kilometre.

div.head: Sample collection and DNA extraction
div.p: Otter spraints were collected along the watercourse on sand banks, rocks, tributary outfalls or banks under bridges. Sampling points were defined considering an equal spatial distribution along the investigated river sections, and finally recorded using a global positioning system unit. We visited these points during three sampling periods for each study site between February and mid April 2011. One sampling period consisted of five consecutive days and all sampling points of one study site were checked daily for fresh spraints from the previous night. To minimise DNA degradation and to maximise DNA amplification success, sampling was carried out mainly during morning hours in cold months (Coxon et al. 1999;Nsubuga et al. 2004;Hájková et al., 2006;Lampa et al., 2008). To avoid cross-contamination only spraints that had no physical contact with other spraints were collected. Samples were stored in plastic tubes with 30 ml of a nucleic acid stabilising reagent (3.53 M ammonium sulphate, 13.3 mM EDTA, 16.6 mM sodium citrate, adjusted to pH 5.2 with 1 M sulphuric acid) and frozen at -20 • C.

DNA extraction was carried out subsequently after every study period. Faecal DNA was extracted using the QIAmp DNA Stool Mini Kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany) following the manufacturer's protocol with slight modifications: increase of final incubation time to 5 min before elution of the DNA extract.

div.head: DNA quantification, identification of otter individuals and pedigree analysis
div.p: To ensure cost-and time-effectiveness as well as data quality we rejected genotyping error-prone samples by exclusion of samples containing target DNA in very low concentrations. Therefore we quantified target DNA in the extracts applying quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) using a SYBR Greenbased assay in a LightCycler 1.0 Instrument (Roche Applied Science, Mannheim, Germany) and the primer system LutRT2, following the protocol of Hausknecht et al. (2010). An absolute quantification was performed with an external calibration curve obtained from three-fold quantification of 17 standards with known DNA concentrations of the target species. Subsequently we determined the DNA concentration of extracts using the equation in Morin et al. (2001) and excluded samples containing <5 pg/L DNA in the extract from further analyses.

Samples were genotyped at 11 microsatellite loci established by Dallas and Piertney (1998) : Lut435, Lut457, Lut615, Lut701, Lut717, Lut833 (set 1) andLut453, Lut604, Lut715, Lut733, Lut832 (set 2). All amplifications were performed in 15 L reactions containing 7.5 L 2× Qiagen Multiplex PCR Master Mix (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany), 0.04 g/L bovine serum albumin (Fermentas, St. Leon-Rot, Germany), 0.2 pmol/L of each primer and 2.5 L template DNA. Microsatellites were amplified in two multiplex PCRs using the following protocol: initial denaturation for 15 min at 95 • C followed by 40 cycles (30 s at 94 • C, 90 s at 55 • C (set 1)/56 • C (set 2), 60 s at 72 • C) and a final extension step for 30 min at 60 • C. Forward primers were labelled with a fluorescent dye (6-FAM, HEX or TAMRA). Fragment length analysis was performed on an ABI Prism ® 377 DNA sequencer (Perkin Elmer, Rodgau, Germany). Genotyping data were analysed using GENESCAN 3.1.2 and GENOTYPER 2.5 software (Applied Biosystems ® , Foster City, USA).

Initially the selected samples were amplified independently in triplicates for all loci and up to 6 additional PCR reactions were performed to determine a sample's consensus genotype if necessary. We accepted a heterozygote genotype when each of both alleles was recorded in at least two independent PCRs and a homozygote genotype after at least three independent observations of a single allele. Accordingly we based the quantification of genotyping errors on consensus genotypes obtained from repeated genotyping. Frequency of allelic dropout (ADO) and false alleles (FA) were computed using the equations in Broquet and Petit (2004) and rates for PCR amplification success, ADO and FA were calculated for each locus across all samples and for each sample across all loci. The probability of identity (P ID ) and probability of identity for siblings (P IDsibs ), which is a more conservative upper bound for the probability of identity (Taberlet and Luikart, 1999;Waits et al., 2001), were calculated using the software GIMLET (Valière, 2002). We used the software GenAlEx 6.5 (Peakall andSmouse, 2006, 2012) to characterise genetic variation within the study sites providing 2).

For sex identification we amplified a part of the SRY locus (Dallas et al., 2000) and the microsatellite Lut832 as a positive PCR control for female samples in a multiplex PCR. A 15 L reaction was performed consisting of 1.5 L PCR buffer, 0.2 mM dNTPs, 3 mM MgCl 2 , 0.04 g/L bovine serum albumin, 0.08 U/L FIREPol ® DNA Polymerase (Solis Biodyne, Tartu, Estonia), 0.2 pmol/L of the microsatellite locus primers, 0.4 pmol/L for Lut-SRY primers and 2 L of template DNA. The PCR programme used: initial denaturation for 3 min at 94 • C, 40 cycles (30 s at 94 • C, 90 s at 53 • C, 30 s at 72 • C) and a final extension step for 3 min at 72 • C.

Individuals defined by assigning a unique multilocus genotype derived from microsatellite and SRY analysis were tested for possible parent-offspring combinations by the complete exclusion method based on Mendelian rules of inheritance. We compared multilocus genotypes to each other and parent-offspring combinations were rejected if a candidate parent does not share at least one allele with the offspring at any locus under consideration (Jones et al., 2010).

We additionally estimated population sizes by capture-markrecapture (CMR) analysis using the programme CAPWIRE (Miller et al., 2005) to evaluate if the detected otter individuals represent the populations adequately in both study sites. This software takes into account multiple capture events per sampling occasion. Otter population size was calculated separately for each study site. A "recapture" was recorded whenever an identical genotype was found in another DNA sample. A likelihood ratio test (p < 0.05) was used to choose between two models concerning capture heterogeneity: the even capture probability model (ECM) and the two innate rates model (TIRM). Confidence intervals were estimated using a parametric bootstrap procedure.

div.head: Prey fish populations
div.p: Size and composition of prey fish populations were estimated based on electrofishing data obtained for stream sections at Kleiner Kamp between 2006 and 2011 and at Große Ysper between 2003 and 2008 (Fig. 1). Although the data sets cover different time periods a comparison is legitimate because in both streams fisheries management did not change throughout the whole period investigated. Sampling stretches (lengths range from 80 to 198 m) were selected to be representative according to habitat distribution. By weighting a representative amount of fish individuals of every length cohort a length-weight relationship formula was created for body mass calculation. All data on fish originated from autumn samplings. For each data set fish biomass was estimated according to DeLury (1951) or Seber and Le Cren (1967), depending on the number of electrofishing runs per stretch. By exploratory data analysis we compared the fish biomass between the studied streams to ascertain tendencies of differences in food availability for otters caused by stocking and tested for differences applying a Mann-Whitney-U-test. Moreover we show length frequency distribution for the dominant species brown trout to analyse population structure for both studied streams.

div.head: Quality of samples and characteristics of genetic markers
div.p: DNA was extracted from a total of 164 otter spraints (68 samples from the study site Kleiner Kamp, 96 from Große Ysper). 77 samples (46.9%) were excluded after DNA quantification as they contained <5 pg/L target DNA. 81 of the samples left were genotyped successfully for all microsatellite loci (i.e. 49.4% of all collected faeces): 33 samples for study site Kleiner Kamp and 48 for Große Ysper. Another 6 samples were rejected due to incomplete genotypes.

Overall all microsatellite loci were polymorphic with the number of alleles per locus ranging from 2 to 5. Expected heterozygosity ranged between 0.48 and 0.53 and observed heterozygosity ranged from 0.54 to 0.61 for the two study sites, respectively (Table 2). These values correspond well to those of values of related studies (e.g. Janssens et al., 2008;Hájková et al., 2009;Honnen et al., 2011). Mean PCR success rate across all loci was 92.0%. Mean frequency of ADO per locus varied from 8.3% for Lut435 to 23.3% for Lut833. FA were recorded with a frequency from 0.3% for Lut715 up to 6.5% for Lut435. P ID and P IDsibs for eleven microsatellite markers based on allele frequencies in our data set were 6.45 × 10 -8 and 1.38 × 10 -3 respectively.

div.head: Otter numbers and sex identification
div.p: Successfully genotyped samples revealed 6 different genotypes (K1-K6) for the study site Kleiner Kamp. From these we identified 3 male otters, 2 females, one not specified. At the study site Große Ysper 8 different otter individuals (Y1-Y8) were detected -3 males and 5 females (Fig. 2). The number of genotyped faeces per individual varied from 1 to 17 (Fig. 2), indicating considerable capture heterogeneity among individuals.

Using the likelihood ratio test for capture heterogeneity, for both study sites the TIRM model was selected (with p = 0.031 for Kleiner Kamp and p = 0.00 for Große Ysper). The CAPWIRE point estimate of population size for Kleiner Kamp site was 6 otters with a 95% confidence interval of zero. This perfectly coincides with the number of detected genotypes. For the second study site Große Ysper the population size estimate generated by CAPWIRE was 8 individuals with an upper confidence boundary of 9 otter individuals. The CAPWIRE point estimate as well as the lower confidence boundary corresponds to the number of genotypes obtained.

div.head: Spatial and social organisation and densities of resident otters
div.p: Among the 14 identified otter individuals 11 were detected over the entire sampling time. They were defined as resident animals. Hence, there were 4 resident otters at study site Kleiner Kamp and 7 residents at study site Große Ysper (Fig. 2). Individuals represented only in a single sampling period and not fitting into the pedigree of resident otters were defined as transient animals.

The stream lengths between the outermost detection points represent minimum home ranges for each otter individual. The spatial distribution found suggests a typical spacing pattern for mustelids (Powell, 1979) with hardly overlapping intrasexual territories and territory overlap between sexes. However, we observed high territory overlaps between individuals of the same sex for Y1/Y4 (♂) and Y5/Y6 (♀). Complete exclusion for parentage analysis based on microsatellite data revealed an existing family group with Y1 and Y5 as parents of two offspring, Y4 and Y6.

We determined otter numbers per stream length using the numbers of otter individuals identified within each study site (Table 1). Focusing on the numbers of resident otters, we found a one-third higher otter density for Große Ysper, the study site where intensive fish stocking is carried out.

div.head: Fish biomass and population status
div.p: Population structure of fish sizes of brown trout indicated natural reproduction and no deficits in the year-class abundances (Fig. 3). According to regions of the epi-and metarhithral fish species composition is dominated by brown trout regarding the fish biomass (Kleiner Kamp: mean 81.5%, Große Ysper: mean 95.1%) as well as abundance (data not shown). For the study site Kleiner Kamp other stock building species bullhead, burbot (Lota lota) and grayling (Thymallus thymallus) were recorded, which made up to 49.5% of fish biomass depending on the stream section. At Große Ysper bullheads were registered as second stock building species.

Despite intensive stocking at Große Ysper, specimen of rainbow trout and brook trout were missing completely or were detected only by single captures. Additionally the proportion of catchable sized brown trout did not differ between the streams (U = 38, p = 0.857) and averaged 28.4% of brown trout biomass in Kleiner Kamp and 27.1% in Große Ysper (Table 3). Comparing fish biomass of all fish species and sizes per year a tendency for a higher fish biomass for study site Große Ysper was recorded, which however, cannot be referred to stocking measures of catchable sized fish (see Fig. 3).

div.head: Discussion
div.p: In this study, we investigated whether stocking of fish into streams influences food availability for otters and therefore affects otter numbers and densities. Contrarily to what we have expected, we found no significant alteration of fish stocks between the streams as indicated by length frequency distribution and biomass of fish -although different fisheries management strategies are implemented and additional food supply in terms of stocked fish theoretically available for otters is high (25-50% of average natural occurring fish biomass). For both streams electrofishing data revealed intact, river-type specific fish populations, whereas stocked specimen were almost missing at the time of electrofishing surveys (autumn). Our findings are supported by numerous studies, showing that survival of stocked hatchery-reared specimen is often much lower, than for wild trout, and that most stocking events are characterized by a large initial mortality and outmigration of stocked specimen within a few weeks (Berg and Jørgensen, 1991;Weber and Fausch, 2003;Aarestrup et al., 2005). Various factors are contributing to this: hatchery-reared fish are not used to natural conditions and show poor foraging and swimming skills and prior residence effects lead to poor survival rates of stocked fish, where natural reproduction of wild trout takes place. Furthermore, hatchery-reared fish exhibit an underdeveloped predator avoidance behaviour (Olla et al., 1998;Petersson and Järvi, 2006). These effects become even more pronounced the longer fish experience the hatchery environment (Pinter, 2008). Linked to these findings, by analysing hard prey remains in otter faeces at the time of stocking events, Poledník et al. (2004) and Jacobsen (2005) could show a shift in species and size distribution of preyed fish towards that of stocked specimen in rivers underlying conventional fisheries management. In case of Poledník et al. (2004) diet composition generally reflected prey fish availability in the streams, whereas Jacobsen (2005) recorded a preference for stocked fish species and sizes.

Usually in surveys on population estimates, otter abundance and density are given as the total number of animals identified along a river section or a shoreline, or are expressed as index values per unit of water area or stream length (Chanin, 2003). Ruiz-Olmo et al. (2011) pointed out that the use of indirect monitoring methods often includes dispersers and cubs, which can be misleading, as data on mammal abundances are commonly presented as number of adult individuals or breeders. Including all resident otter individuals identified within the particular case study areas our results show a higher otter density for the stream where fish stocking takes place. However, taking into account information on sex, kinship and individual spatial distribution, we have strong evidence for an existing family group with probably two juvenile individuals within the study area Große Ysper. According to Ruiz-Olmo et al. (2005, 2011) otters are breeding more successfully in areas with higher food abundance and females with cubs use rich feeding patches. However, as solitary and territorial species, young otters are supposed to leave the natal range after disbandment of the family group to search for own territories (Kruuk, 2006). This has to be considered when calculating otter densities. Concerning our study, after dispersal of the offspring, both streams investigated show similar otter density values (Kleiner Kamp: 0.22 otters/km; Große Ysper: 0.23 otters/km).

In recent studies (Koelewijn et al., 2010;Quaglietta et al., 2013) dispersal behaviour was not shown in context of food availability, but Quaglietta et al. (2013) suggest that dispersal behaviour is not only based on biologically intrinsic mechanisms like inbreeding avoidance, but also reflects density-dependent mechanisms (especially concerning dispersal distances). Albeit they recorded short dispersal distances for otters (Quaglietta et al. 2013: dispersal from 11 to 25 km for four subadult male otters; no dispersal detected for two subadult females), they did not detect any potential breeding pair composed of related adults. Accordantly in literature we found no example of offspring staying within the natal area after disbandment of the family group, regardless of prey availability. Hence, also following Erlinge (1968) and Ó Néill et al. (2009), we adhere to the assumption that dispersal, ranging behaviour and therefore also control of population density mainly relies on the social and spatial organisation of adult otters.

Apart from socio-biological restrictions in this territorial species, it is considered that otters are food-limited: Kruuk et al. (1993) found a high correlation between utilisation of streams by otters and biomass of fish and Lanszki et al. (2010) reported more than two-fold higher otter density in a fish pond system with three times higher prey supply than in a second fish pond system. Further, Ruiz-Olmo et al. ( 2011) showed a higher density of adult otters and a higher number of large cubs per year linked with food abundance. As demonstrated by Sulkava (2006) especially changes in continuity and stability of food resources can cause intraspecific competition, e.g. when ice cover during winter excludes resident otter individuals from feeding patches. In case of the study area Kleiner Kamp constant, predictable food availability in terms of wild fish stocks can be assumed across all years and throughout a year (Unfer, personal observation, 2011). On the contrary, in anthropogenically influenced systems like Große Ysper, stocking of fish during the angling season leads to considerable fluctuations in food availability. Hence, concerning food availability for otters, we presume that the limiting factor would be the time span after the angling season (autumn, winter) when no additional prey in terms of stocked fish enters the water.

In conclusion, taking the example of our study sites, compared to otter habitats hardly influenced by human activities, it appears that there is no increase of otter territories according to typical spacing patterns for mustelids following Powell (1979) in areas where fish stocking takes place. Concordantly, we could show a trend suggesting fish stocking does not play a role in food availability for otters -at least not on the long term. Therefore we assume that stocking may not affect otter densities in the observed streams, because additional food supply is not constantly available to raise the carrying capacity for otters permanently. Nevertheless, in times of rearing the offspring stocked fish may be an easy prey for lactating females and young inexperienced otters and, thus, fish stocking possibly increases reproductive success and consequently also dispersal rates of the young.

Albeit problems in the context of fish stocking are well known (e.g. Aarestrup et al., 2005;Baer et al., 2007), it is still practiced in many European rivers and conflicts with fish-eating predators are also widespread. Our study outlines interactions between fisheries management strategies, fish stocks and otter densities. The application of non-invasive genetic sampling methods in combination with capture-mark-recapture models proved to be a valuable monitoring tool for otter census, because it supplies additional data on social and spatial organisation of detected individuals. In our study we found very similar otter densities along the two studied streams concerning otters' territories. Considering that fisheries management practices have not changed in the past two to three decades, we can assume that the current number of detected otter territories reflects the carrying capacity for adult resident otters along the investigated stream sections. However, during the time of fish stocking the additional food resources will likely be used also by transient otter individuals and may enhance reproductive success of breeding females. Nevertheless, in our case study we found no evidence that stocking of fish raises otter densities in terms of number of otter territories along a stream.

Our findings on fish stocks and otter densities support the assumption that stocking of fish is inefficient, especially in streams where both self-sustaining fish populations and fish-eating predators occur. Furthermore we could show that otter predation does not harm the river-type specific fish populations of the studied streams. However, the impact of otters on commercially valuable stocked fish, their relative importance and contribution to otter diets as well as selectivity of otters for stocked hatchery-reared fish still remain poorly understood. In order to elucidate the contribution of stocked fish to otter diet, it would be necessary to implement dietary analyses (e.g. scat and stomach analysis, stable isotopes) and run an experimental study specifically designed to ascertain prey availability, otters' resource use and density simultaneously. Thus, to quantify the contribution of stocked fish to otter diet and to evaluate the effects on otter population dynamics in more detail further investigations -especially long-term studies -are urgently needed and recommended.
